passages.happening:
“After this I saw another angel descending from heaven with great authority, and the earth was illuminated by his glory” (verse 1).

He cries out in a mighty voice: “Fallen, fallen is Babylon the great! She has become a lair for demons and a haunt for every unclean spirit, every unclean bird, and every detestable beast” (verse 2).

“All the nations have drunk the wine of the passion of her immorality. The kings of the earth were immoral with her, and the merchants of the earth have grown wealthy from the extravagance of her luxury” (verse 3).
passages.hearers:
Chapter 17 showed who Babylon is. Chapter 18 shows her fall, and it does so almost entirely through voices. There is no battle scene. We hear an angel's announcement, a call to God's people, three laments from those who grew rich from her, a call to heaven, and a closing song of silence. Her fall was announced in 14:8 and carried out under the seventh bowl in 16:19. This chapter lets the reader feel what it means.

The angel's glory lights up the earth. Babylon's splendour was borrowed and paid for by others. This light comes from heaven.

His cry repeats Isaiah's word over the first Babylon: ‘Fallen, fallen’. The city that was full of music, trade and feasting becomes a ruin where only unclean creatures live.

Verse 3 names three groups who will speak in this chapter: the nations, drunk on her wine; the kings, who shared her bed; and the merchants, who grew rich from her luxury. Her power was political and religious, and it was also economic. The Greek word for merchant, emporos, from which English gets ‘emporium’, means a wholesale trader who travels by sea.
passages.ot:
The cry is Isaiah's: “Fallen, fallen is Babylon! All the images of her gods lie shattered on the ground!” (Isaiah 21:9).

And the cup that made the nations drunk is Jeremiah's: “Babylon was a gold cup in the hand of the LORD, making the whole earth drunk” (Jeremiah 51:7).
passages.asks: Ask what in your own world looks permanent and splendid but is borrowed and paid for by others. Ask what it means that the light in this chapter comes from heaven, not from the city. And ask which of the three groups, the drunk, the powerful or the profiting, you are most like.

passages.happening:
John hears another voice from heaven: “Come out of her, My people, so that you will not share in her sins or contract any of her plagues. For her sins are piled up to heaven, and God has remembered her iniquities” (verses 4-5).

“Give back to her as she has done to others; pay her back double for what she has done; mix her a double portion in her own cup” (verse 6). “As much as she has glorified herself and lived in luxury, give her the same measure of torment and grief. In her heart she says, ‘I sit as queen; I am not a widow and will never see grief’” (verse 7).

“Therefore her plagues will come in one day— death and grief and famine— and she will be consumed by fire, for mighty is the Lord God who judges her” (verse 8).
passages.hearers:
‘Come out of her, My people’ is the heart of the chapter. It is the call Jeremiah gave to the exiles in the real Babylon. Here it is spoken to the churches.

What does it mean to come out? It is a call to separate from Babylon's sins, not necessarily to leave a place. God's people live inside the economy and culture around them, as the exiles did in Babylon. They are asked to refuse its idolatry and its injustice, so that they do not share in its sins. For the churches of Asia, that touched the trade guilds and their banquets, the marketplace, and the worship that went with them. The letters to Thyatira and Laodicea already raised this question.

‘Her sins are piled up to heaven, and God has remembered.’ The powerful think that what they have done is forgotten. God does not forget.

Then her pride speaks. ‘I sit as queen; I am not a widow and will never see grief.’ Babylon in Isaiah said nearly the same words. It is the voice of a power that believes itself safe for ever. The Greek word for living in luxury, strēniaō, suggests proud, self-indulgent excess that thinks it is beyond reach. And what she thought could never happen comes ‘in one day’.
passages.ot:
The call is Jeremiah's: “Come out of her, My people! Save your lives, each of you, from the fierce anger of the LORD” (Jeremiah 51:45).

The boast is Isaiah's Babylon: “So now hear this, O lover of luxury who sits securely, who says to herself, ‘I am, and there is none besides me. I will never be a widow or know the loss of children’” (Isaiah 47:8).

And the language of double payment is the prophets': “And I will first repay them double their iniquity and their sin” (Jeremiah 16:18).
passages.hard:
‘Pay her back double.’ Is this a call to revenge?

Many readers find these words hard, and they are right to notice them. Several things help. The command to repay is not spoken to Christians. It is addressed to heaven's agents of God's justice. Revelation never asks believers to take revenge, and the New Testament forbids it: “Do not avenge yourselves, beloved, but leave room for God’s wrath” (Romans 12:19). Many scholars think ‘double’ here is an idiom drawn from the prophets for full or matching payment, rather than a demand for twice the harm. And the reason given is plain: she is to receive ‘as she has done to others’. Judgment fits the wrong.

Readers still differ on how much of this language belongs to the prophets' way of speaking and how much is to be taken plainly. On every reading, the chapter's concern is that the victims of injustice are finally seen and set right.
passages.asks: Ask where Babylon's ways have reached into your own life: your spending, your work, your sense of what makes a life secure. Ask what it would mean for you to ‘come out of her’ while still living and working where you are. And ask where you hear the voice that says ‘I sit as queen’, in yourself, your church or your culture.

passages.happening:
The kings who lived in luxury with her “will weep and wail at the sight of the smoke rising from the fire that consumes her” (verse 9). Standing far off in fear, they cry: “Woe, woe to the great city, the mighty city of Babylon! For in a single hour your judgment has come” (verse 10).

“And the merchants of the earth will weep and mourn over her, because there is no one left to buy their cargo” (verse 11). John lists the cargo: gold, silver, jewels and pearls; fine linen, purple, silk and scarlet; citron wood, ivory, bronze, iron and marble; cinnamon, spice, incense, myrrh and frankincense; wine, oil, flour and wheat; cattle, sheep, horses and chariots; “of slaves and souls of men” (verses 12-13). The merchants cry, “Woe, woe to the great city” and “For in a single hour such fabulous wealth has been destroyed!” (verses 16-17).

“Every shipmaster, passenger, and sailor, and all who make their living from the sea, will stand at a distance” (verse 17). “Then they will throw dust on their heads as they weep and mourn and cry out: ‘Woe, woe to the great city, where all who had ships on the sea were enriched by her wealth! For in a single hour she has been destroyed’” (verse 19).
passages.hearers:
Three groups mourn: the kings, the merchants and the seafarers. Each lament begins ‘Woe, woe to the great city’ and ends ‘in a single hour’, so that they sound like a chorus at a funeral. The prophets used funeral songs like this, with bitter irony, for cities that thought themselves immortal. ‘Woe’, ouai, is both a cry of grief and a word of doom at once.

Each group ‘stands at a distance’. They want no share in her fire. And notice what they grieve. Not the people who died. They grieve lost trade. ‘There is no one left to buy their cargo.’

The cargo list reads like a customs record of the Roman world. Rome imported huge quantities of goods through its port at Ostia, at the mouth of the Tiber: grain from Egypt and North Africa, spices and silk from the east, ivory from Africa and India, marble from Greece and Asia Minor. Wealthy Romans paid fortunes for tables of citron wood from North Africa. Cities of Asia such as Laodicea and Ephesus took part in this trade, so some of John's first hearers lived by it.

The list ends with a jarring phrase: ‘slaves and souls of men’. Slavery held up the Roman economy, and slaves were traded as cargo, beside cattle and horses. The last item tells the truth about all the others. A system that will sell anything ends by selling people.

Throwing dust on the head was a common gesture of grief in the ancient world. The whole scene is modelled on Ezekiel's lament over Tyre, the great merchant city of the Phoenician coast.
passages.ot:
The laments follow Ezekiel's over Tyre: “How you have perished, O city of renown inhabited by seafaring men” (Ezekiel 26:17). The sailors there too “will throw dust on their heads and roll in ashes” (Ezekiel 27:30).

And Tyre's cargo, like Babylon's, included people: “Javan, Tubal, and Meshech were your merchants. They exchanged slaves and bronze utensils for your merchandise” (Ezekiel 27:13).
passages.hard:
Did this happen? And who is the city?

Rome was not destroyed in a single hour in John's lifetime. Part of it burned in the great fire of AD 64 under Nero, and it was sacked by the Visigoths in AD 410 and again by the Vandals in AD 455, though the city went on. Readers take the chapter in the four ways the book page sets out, and these notes do not choose. Preterists see it as the prophetic verdict on first-century Rome, or, for some, on Jerusalem. Historicists have traced it through later events in the history of the West. Futurists expect a final world city or economic system to fall at the end. Idealists read it as God's verdict on every economy of exploitation, carried out again and again in history and finally at its end. The notes on chapter 17 say more, and these notes name no city, nation or economy of our own day as Babylon.

The chapter's question for every reader is the merchants' question turned around: what do we mourn when it is lost, people or things?

A word for anyone who is being held, owned or forced to work today. It is not your fault. You are not the property of the people who hold you. If you can, please tell someone you trust and get help. The Find Help page on this site lists places to turn.
passages.asks: Ask what you would grieve most if the wealth around you vanished in an hour. Ask where in the things you buy ‘slaves and souls of men’ might still be part of the cargo. And ask whether you stand close enough to the suffering of others to mourn them, or only at a distance.

passages.t: The millstone, and the silent city
passages.happening:
Then a call goes up: “Rejoice over her, O heaven, O saints and apostles and prophets, because God has pronounced for you His judgment against her” (verse 20).

“Then a mighty angel picked up a stone the size of a great millstone and cast it into the sea, saying: ‘With such violence the great city of Babylon will be cast down, never to be seen again’” (verse 21).

The angel goes on: the sound of harpists and musicians, flute players and trumpeters, “will never ring out in you again. Nor will any craftsmen of any trade be found in you again, nor the sound of a millstone be heard in you again” (verse 22). “The light of a lamp will never shine in you again, and the voices of a bride and bridegroom will never call out in you again. For your merchants were the great ones of the earth, because all the nations were deceived by your sorcery” (verse 23).

“And there was found in her the blood of prophets and saints, and of all who had been slain on the earth” (verse 24).
passages.hearers:
The millstone is a prophet's sign. Jeremiah told a messenger to tie his scroll of judgment to a stone and throw it into the Euphrates, as a sign that Babylon would sink and never rise. Here a mighty angel throws a stone the size of a great millstone into the sea.

Then the angel's song of silence. One by one the ordinary sounds of a city stop: music, craftsmen at work, the millstone grinding grain, a lamp in a window, the voices of a bride and bridegroom. The word ‘again’ rings through the verses like a bell. These were the sounds of any town. Jeremiah had used the same list for the silence of judgment on Judah. The picture is not meant to be enjoyed. It is meant to show what is lost when a civilization is built on deceit and blood.

And the last verse gives the reason. In her was found ‘the blood of prophets and saints, and of all who had been slain on the earth’. Not only Christians. All who had been killed. God judges a power for all the innocent blood it has shed.

The book does not end with this silence. The city that replaces Babylon in chapters 21 and 22 has its own lamp, the Lamb, and its own bride. Its glory costs no one their life.
passages.ot:
The stone is Jeremiah's sign: “When you finish reading this scroll, tie a stone to it and cast it into the Euphrates. Then you are to say, ‘In the same way Babylon will sink and never rise again’” (Jeremiah 51:63-64).

And the silence is Jeremiah's: “Moreover, I will banish from them the sounds of joy and gladness, the voices of the bride and bridegroom, the sound of the millstones, and the light of the lamp” (Jeremiah 25:10).
passages.hard:
How can heaven be told to rejoice over a city's fall?

The call to rejoice sounds harsh to many readers. The rejoicing is over justice done, not over suffering as such. God has judged a power that shed the blood of prophets, of saints, and of all who had been slain on the earth. The Old Testament often calls God's people to rejoice when oppressors fall, because that fall is their rescue. And the call is answered in chapter 19 not with taunts but with worship of God.

The chapter is sober. Its last word is not joy at others' pain but the blood of the innocent, finally found and finally answered.
passages.asks: Ask which ordinary sounds of your own life, music, work, a lamp at night, a wedding, you most take for granted. Ask what it means to you that God counts the blood of ‘all who had been slain on the earth’. And ask how you can rejoice in God's justice without rejoicing in anyone's pain.
